title: Short Stuff: Nicknames
summary: Short Stuff episode on the origins of common English nicknames. Josh and Chuck walk through how names like Chuck (Charles), Hank (Henry), Dick/Rick and Hick (Richard), Bob/Hob/Dob (Robert), Bill (William), Peggy and Maggie (Margaret), Daisy (Margaret), Moth/Patsy (Martha), Nancy (Ann), Sally (Sarah), and Jack (John) came about, including rhyming-name fads, Dutch and French influences, and suffix theories. The hosts note that the origin of Jack is uncertain and that the origin of Chuck is murky, centered on a Chinatown figure named George Washington O'Connor.

segments.title: Opening and Chuck origin
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the nickname topic and explain that Chuck is short for Charles, tracing it to a Chinatown figure George Washington O'Connor, whose nickname may have come from Chuck steak, with the hosts noting the story is murky.

segments.title: Hank, Henry and Dutch influence
segments.summary: Hank is discussed as a short form of Henry, with the Dutch name Hank (Henk) used in New York among Dutch settlers. The hosts note Harry was the common English nickname for Henry, and Prince Harry's real name is Henry.

segments.title: Richard, Dick and Hick; rhyming names
segments.summary: Medieval England had few common given names, so people used nicknames to tell apart men with the same name. Rhyming names with changed initial letters were popular, so Richard became Hick and later Dick. Robert similarly was Hob or Dob before Bob, which explains surnames like Hobson and Dobson.

segments.title: William to Bill and Margaret nicknames
segments.summary: Bill for William is linked to Irish Gaelic pronunciation, where the W sound becomes a buzz, so William the Conqueror was called Billy in Ireland. Margaret becomes Peggy and Maggie through a rhyming fad in the sixteenth century. Margaret also became Daisy via French marguerite.

segments.title: Martha, Ann and Sarah nicknames
segments.summary: Martha evolved through Moth and Maddie to Patty and Patsy. Ann became Nan, then Nancy, via a phrase like 'mine Ann'. Sarah became Sally, possibly from children's difficulty pronouncing R.

segments.title: Hosts' personal anecdotes on nicknames
segments.summary: Chuck describes his daughter's imaginary friends with nicknames like Salsa, Fossil, Andy, See Saw and See You, and his oldest sister's imaginary friends Bobby Teak and Peak.

segments.title: John and Jack
segments.summary: Jack as a nickname for John is discussed. One theory links it to Norman French Jacques, but Jacques is the French form of James, so it is doubtful. Another theory involves the medieval suffix -kin, giving Jenkin, shortened to Jink, then Jack. The hosts conclude no one knows for sure.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listeners to share their nicknames and sign off; the episode closes with production credits.
